blocks.body: Kerberoasting: TGS ticket bursts. Pass-the-hash: stolen NTLM hash reused. DCSync: fake replication pulls hashes. DCShadow: rogue DC injects changes.
Tiered administration (0/1/2), LAPS unique local passwords, Credential Guard, phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2, Windows Hello).
Password hash sync, pass-through authentication, or federation. PIM for just-in-time privileged roles; access reviews to revoke the unjustified.
OSI: 7 layers. TCP/IP: 4 layers. Map each attack class to the layer where it lives before placing controls.
SHA-2 family for integrity; salt passwords (rainbow tables); file-integrity monitoring; MD5 is dead (collisions).
Symmetric: one shared key (bulk data). Asymmetric: public/private pair (key exchange, identity). PKI binds identities to keys via certificates.
Compare against the vendor's published digest before installing.
At rest: disk/volume encryption. In transit: TLS. In use: memory protections. Key management is the real work.
Learning mode (baseline) -> policy design -> approval workflows -> enforcement. Never enforce on day one.
Per app, restrict: app-to-app communication, file/registry access, network egress. Browsers, Office, scripting hosts first - that is where LOLBins live.
Living-off-the-land binaries (PowerShell et al.): legitimate tools weaponized without malware. Ringfencing contains them.
Just-in-time elevation: rights granted temporarily, then removed. USB/removable media: policy decides which devices, users, data.
Triage fast, contain with playbooks, run the post-incident learning loop - each incident becomes a control.

cheatSheets.title: NIST SP 800-207 — the seven tenets, cold

blocks.body: All data sources and computing services are resources. All communication is secured regardless of network location.
Access to individual enterprise resources is granted on a per-session basis. Access is determined by dynamic policy — including observable state of client identity, application, and asset.

The enterprise monitors and measures the integrity and security posture of all owned and associated assets. All resource authentication and authorization are dynamic and strictly enforced before access.
The enterprise collects as much information as possible about the current state of assets, network infrastructure, and communications, and uses it to improve its security posture.
Policy engine (decides) → policy administrator (executes) → policy enforcement point/PEP (carries out). Control plane vs data plane separation.

cheatSheets.title: AD attack paths — how it gets hacked

blocks.body: Kerberoasting: crackable TGS for SPN accounts. AS-REP roasting: accounts without pre-auth. Golden ticket: krbtgt hash → forged TGT. Silver ticket: service account hash → forged TGS.
LSASS dumping (Mimikatz), NTDS.dit extraction, DCSync replication abuse. One DA hash = domain compromise.
SID history injection, cross-forest trust exploitation, unconstrained delegation (impersonate anyone connecting).
Tiered admin model (no DA on workstations), LAPS for local admins, Protected Users group, disable unconstrained delegation, monitor replication anomalies.
Default-deny execution: only approved binaries run. Learning/audit mode first to baseline, then enforce. Hash + publisher + path rules.
Constrain what allowed apps can *do*: block Word from spawning PowerShell, browsers from writing to startup folders. Application behavior control.
Block unapproved USB/mass storage or force encryption. Data can't leave on what can't mount.
Just-in-time admin rights with approval workflow and full audit — standing local admin is the vulnerability.
Pilot group → monitor breaks → tune → expand. Default-deny done badly is a self-inflicted DoS.

cheatSheets.title: Entra ID & Conditional Access — the identity plane

blocks.body: Join/register devices → provision users (HR-driven) → assign access (groups, roles) → review (access reviews) → deprovision. Joiner-mover-leaver automated.
IF signal (user, device, location, risk) THEN require (MFA, compliant device, terms). Policies are ANDed; test in report-only mode first.
Phishing-resistant first: FIDO2, Windows Hello for Business, CBA. Push MFA < number matching < phishing-resistant. Kill SMS where possible.
Entra Connect syncs AD → Entra ID. Pass-through vs hash sync vs federation — know the auth path your org actually uses.

answerBank.q: Is this course affiliated with ThreatLocker?
answerBank.a: No. It is distilled from the public shape of ThreatLocker's no-cost Zero Trust Cybersecurity Bootcamp as an independent companion - not affiliated with or endorsed by ThreatLocker.

answerBank.q: Does completing this academy confer a certification?
answerBank.a: No. Preparation only - this course confers no certificate. Vendor certification exams are taken through the vendor's own portal.

answerBank.q: What is the core doctrine of the academy?
answerBank.a: Never trust, always verify - the tagline and the Zero Trust principle: assume breach, verify every request, enforce least privilege by default-deny.

answerBank.q: Which NIST publication anchors the Zero Trust material?
answerBank.a: NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture - the seven tenets, the policy engine / policy administrator / PEP logical model, and continuous diagnostics.

answerBank.q: What does the SC-300 path cover?
answerBank.a: Entra ID identity lifecycle (joiner-mover-leaver, B2B, access packages), Zero Trust Conditional Access, authentication and authorization (MFA, passwordless, OAuth2/OIDC/SAML), hybrid identity, governance (PIM, access reviews), and troubleshooting with PowerShell and KQL.

The ZTA logical trio: engine decides, administrator executes, enforcement point carries out.
Five pillars (identity, devices, networks, applications, data) scored Traditional → Advanced → Optimal.

Constraining the behaviors of allowed applications (child processes, network, file writes).
Just-in-time privileged access with approval and audit instead of standing admin rights.
Offline cracking of Kerberos service tickets for accounts with SPNs.
Pulling domain hashes via replication rights — mimicking a domain controller.
AD setting letting a service impersonate any connecting user to any service — prime attack path.
Separating Tier 0 (domain), Tier 1 (servers), Tier 2 (workstations) credentials so one compromise can't escalate.
Local Administrator Password Solution: unique, rotated local admin passwords per machine.
Microsoft's cloud identity platform (formerly Azure AD): users, groups, Conditional Access, hybrid sync.
Policy engine: if signals (user/device/location/risk), then require controls (MFA, compliance).
FIDO2, Windows Hello, certificate auth — not phishable like SMS or push.
AD + Entra ID synchronized via Entra Connect: one identity across on-prem and cloud.
Microsoft Identity and Access Administrator certification: Entra ID, CA, governance.
Integrity: data unaltered (hashing/MACs). Confidentiality: data unreadable (encryption). Different goals, different primitives.

faq.q: Is Zero Trust a product I can buy?
faq.a: No — it's an architecture and operating discipline (NIST SP 800-207). Vendors sell components (identity, EDR, microsegmentation); the maturity model measures how completely you've implemented the tenets.

faq.q: Allowlisting sounds like it will break everything. How do real orgs deploy it?
faq.a: Learning/audit mode first: baseline what's actually executed for 2–4 weeks, build policy from evidence, pilot on a tolerant group, then enforce. The course's rollout module walks this sequence.

faq.q: What's the difference between ringfencing and allowlisting?
faq.a: Allowlisting decides *what may run*. Ringfencing decides *what running apps may do*. You need both: an allowed Word spawning PowerShell is the classic bypass.

faq.q: Why is SMS MFA considered weak?
faq.a: SIM-swapping and SS7 interception let attackers receive your codes. Move to phishing-resistant methods (FIDO2/WHfB); at minimum use number-matching push, never SMS, for privileged accounts.

faq.q: Golden ticket vs silver ticket — which should I fear more?
faq.a: Golden (krbtgt compromise) is total domain dominance; silver (service-account hash) is stealthier but scoped to one service. Harden against both: protect krbtgt (rotate twice) and use managed service accounts.

faq.q: How does Conditional Access actually evaluate?
faq.a: All applicable policies combine with AND logic under default-deny. Test every change in report-only mode first — a bad CA policy locks out the organization, including admins (keep break-glass accounts excluded).
SC-300 (identity) if your role is identity/admin; SC-200 (SOC/Sentinel) if you're operations. IL-11 targets SC-300; IL-06 targets SC-200. Identity-first is the Zero Trust order.

faq.q: How is this different from IL-24/IL-29 (ThreatLocker courses)?
faq.a: IL-11 teaches the *doctrine and identity plane* (NIST, CISA, AD, Entra). IL-24/IL-29 teach *operating a default-deny endpoint platform* (ThreatLocker) with assessment/interview prep. Doctrine first, platform second.

tips: Follow the guided path in order — each module unlocks the next. The sequence is the curriculum; skipping ahead breaks the chain.

This course maps to Microsoft Certified: Identity and Access Administrator Associate (SC-300) and Microsoft Certified: Cybersecurity Architect Expert (SC-100) (independent preparation — no affiliation). Weight your drill time toward the heaviest exam domains shown in the cert gates.
The math modules (Number Theory & Modular Arithmetic, Logic & Boolean Algebra) are load-bearing — finish them before the applied modules that assume them.
Quiz-gated modules need 70%+ to unlock the next. When you miss a question, ask Noah to walk you through the miss Socratically before re-attempting.
Do each hands-on lab twice — once following the guide, once from a blank screen. The second pass is where the skill sticks.
This is a 155-hour course: at 10 focused hours a week it takes about 4 months. Short daily sessions beat weekend cramming — pace it like a semester.
